docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
GameDevDocs is a documentation site covering the core concepts behind game development and real-time rendering. This site focuses on the fundamental techniques and theory that apply across all engines and APIs — not engine specific features or workflows.

Whether you are just getting started or looking to deepen your understanding of how things work under the hood, this site aims to be a clear and thorough reference.

docs.title: What This Site Covers
docs.text:
• Rendering — How images are produced from 3D scenes, including rasterization, ray tracing, lighting models, and post processing effects
  • Display Technology — How frames are delivered to your screen, including VSync, adaptive sync, and refresh rate concepts
  • Shading — How surfaces interact with light, including physically based rendering, shadows, and ambient occlusion
  • Anti-Aliasing — Techniques for smoothing jagged edges in rendered images
  • GPU Pipelines — How the graphics pipeline processes geometry and fragments from input to final pixel output

docs.title: What This Site Does Not Cover
docs.text: This site does not cover engine specific implementations or workflows such as Unity, Unreal, or Godot specific menus and settings. The goal is to explain the underlying concepts so you can understand and apply them in any environment.

docs.title: How to Use This Site
docs.text: Use the navigation on the left to browse topics. Each page covers a single concept in full detail, from a basic explanation through to technical depth. Topics are written to be self contained so you can read them in any order.

docs.title: About
docs.text: GameDevDocs is an independent documentation project. All content is original and written with the goal of being accurate, thorough, and accessible to developers at any level.

docs.title: The Frame Buffer
docs.text: The Frame Buffer is a specialized region of Video RAM (VRAM) that contains the complete bitmapped image that will be sent to the display. It acts as the final destination for all rendering operations.

docs.title: How it Works
docs.text:
The Frame Buffer isn't just one block of data; it is composed of several "planes" of information that determine the final color and visibility of every pixel on your screen.

  • Color Buffer: Stores the final RGB values for each pixel.
  • Depth Buffer (Z-Buffer): Manages which objects are in front of others.
  • Stencil Buffer: Used to "mask" certain areas of the screen (e.g., to create portals, reflections, or UI overlays).

docs.title: Double & Triple Buffering
docs.text: To prevent visual artifacts, modern graphics systems use multiple frame buffers.

docs.title: The Problem: Screen Tearing
docs.text: If the GPU writes to the Frame Buffer at the same time the monitor is reading from it, the monitor might display the top half of a new frame and the bottom half of an old frame. This is known as Screen Tearing.

docs.title: The Solution: Double Buffering
docs.text:
Instead of one buffer, the GPU uses two:

  1. The Front Buffer: The one currently being "read" by the monitor.
  2. The Back Buffer: The one the GPU is currently "writing" to.

Once the GPU finishes drawing the entire frame in the Back Buffer, it performs a Swap (or "Flip"), turning the Back Buffer into the Front Buffer.

docs.title: Buffer Operations
docs.text:
Before a new frame can be drawn, the Frame Buffer must undergo several operations:

  1. Clear: The color buffer is reset to a "clear color" (usually black or the sky color), and the depth buffer is reset to infinity.
  2. Draw: The rasterizer fills the pixels based on geometry and shaders.
  3. Blending: If an object is transparent, the GPU calculates a mix between the current pixel color and the new color.
  4. Swap: The finished image is sent to the display.

docs.title: Frame Buffer vs. G-Buffer
docs.text:
It is easy to confuse these two, but they serve different roles in the pipeline:

Feature G-Buffer (Geometry) Frame Buffer Purpose Stores "raw data" for lighting. Stores the final image for display. Visibility You never see this directly. This is exactly what you see on screen. Content Normals, Albedo, Depth, etc. Final Lit Pixels (RGB). Usage Intermediate step in Deferred Rendering. Final step in all rendering.

!!! tip "Memory Tip" The size of the Frame Buffer is directly tied to your Resolution and Bit Depth. Rendering at 4K requires a significantly larger Frame Buffer than rendering at 1080p, which is why VRAM usage spikes at higher resolutions.

docs.title: Geometry Buffer (G-Buffer)
docs.text: The G-Buffer is a collection of textures used in Deferred Rendering to store geometric information about a scene. Instead of calculating lighting immediately for every triangle, the renderer "defers" the lighting until a second pass, using the data stored in these buffers.

docs.title: Why use a G-Buffer?
docs.text:
In traditional "Forward Rendering," if two triangles overlap, the GPU might calculate the lighting for the triangle in the back, only to have the front triangle draw over it later. This is called Overdraw and it wastes performance.

The G-Buffer solves this by rendering the scene's properties once, then calculating lighting only for the pixels that are actually visible to the camera.

docs.title: Standard G-Buffer Components
docs.text: A typical G-Buffer consists of several screen-sized textures, each storing a different piece of information:

docs.title: 1. Diffuse / Albedo Buffer
docs.text: Stores the "base color" of the objects without any lighting or shadows applied. It is essentially what the world would look like under perfectly flat, ambient light.

docs.title: 2. Normal Buffer
docs.text: Stores the world-space or view-space Surface Normals ($x, y, z$ directions). This tells the lighting engine which way each pixel is facing so it can calculate how light should bounce off it.

docs.title: 3. Depth Buffer (Z-Buffer)
docs.text: Stores the distance from the camera to the object. This is critical for positioning light sources in 3D space relative to the surfaces and for generating shadows.

docs.title: 4. Specular / Roughness Buffer
docs.text: Stores material properties, such as how "shiny" or "rough" a surface is. In a PBR (Physically Based Rendering) workflow, this might also include a "Metallic" map.

docs.title: Pass 1: Geometry Pass
docs.text: The scene is rendered, and instead of a final image, the GPU outputs data into the textures mentioned above. At the end of this pass, no lighting has been calculated yet.

docs.title: Pass 2: Lighting Pass
docs.text:
The GPU looks at every pixel in the G-Buffer. It takes the Normal, the Depth, and the Color, then calculates the final lighting for that single pixel.

!!! success "The Advantage" Because lighting is calculated in "screen space" during the second pass, the complexity of the scene depends on the resolution of the screen, not the number of triangles in the scene. This allows for hundreds of dynamic lights in a single frame.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Weakness Description Memory Bandwidth Writing to 4-5 textures at once is very heavy on GPU memory. Transparency G-Buffers struggle with glass or water because they can only store data for one "layer" of depth per pixel. Anti-Aliasing Traditional MSAA (Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing) is difficult to implement with a G-Buffer; most games use TAA or FXAA instead.

docs.title: FXAA (Fast Approximate Anti-Aliasing)
docs.text: FXAA is a post-processing anti-aliasing technique used in games to reduce jagged edges after a frame has already been rendered. Instead of increasing geometry samples like older anti-aliasing methods, FXAA analyzes the final image and smooths visible edges using a fullscreen shader pass. It is known for being lightweight, fast, and effective on weaker hardware.

docs.title: What Is Aliasing?
docs.text: Aliasing happens when diagonal or curved lines appear jagged because screens are made of square pixels. Since pixels cannot perfectly represent smooth angles, edges often look stair-stepped.

docs.title: Why FXAA Was Created
docs.text:
Traditional anti-aliasing methods such as MSAA improve image quality but require more GPU power. This can lower frame rates, especially on older systems.

FXAA was designed to solve that problem by offering:

  • Fast performance
  • Low GPU cost
  • Easy implementation
  • Full-screen smoothing
  • Better FPS on lower-end hardware

docs.title: How FXAA Works
docs.text: FXAA works after the scene has already been rendered.

docs.title: Step 1: Render the Scene
docs.text:
The game renders the normal frame first.

After that, FXAA receives the completed image.

docs.title: Step 2: Detect Edges
docs.text:
FXAA scans nearby pixels and looks for brightness contrast. Strong contrast usually means an edge is present.

Black Black White
Black Black White
Black Black White

docs.title: Step 3: Detect Edge Direction
docs.text:
Once an edge is found, FXAA determines whether it is:

  • Horizontal
  • Vertical
  • Diagonal

This allows smoothing in the correct direction.

docs.title: Step 4: Blend Pixels
docs.text:
FXAA blends neighboring pixels along the edge to soften harsh transitions.

Before:

Black White
Black White
Black White

After:

Black Gray
Black LightGray
Black White

This creates the illusion of a smoother line.

docs.title: Why It Is Called Approximate
docs.text:
FXAA does not calculate real extra geometry samples. Instead, it estimates where edges are based on contrast in the final image.

!!! info "Approximate Means Fast" FXAA trades some accuracy for speed and efficiency.

docs.title: Performance Cost
docs.text:
FXAA is one of the cheapest anti-aliasing methods available.

Typical impact:

  • One fullscreen shader pass
  • Very low GPU usage
  • Excellent for high FPS gaming
  • Ideal for weaker systems

docs.title: Very Fast
docs.text: FXAA has minimal performance cost.

docs.title: Smooths the Entire Image
docs.text:
It can reduce aliasing on:

  • Polygon edges
  • Transparent textures
  • Fences
  • Grass
  • Shader effects

docs.title: Great for Older PCs
docs.text: Excellent when GPU power is limited.

docs.title: Easy to Add
docs.text: Because it is post-processing, developers can implement it easily.

docs.title: Blur
docs.text:
The biggest weakness of FXAA is softness.

It may reduce sharpness on:

  • Text
  • Fine textures
  • User interfaces

docs.title: Lower Quality Than Newer Methods
docs.text: Modern methods like SMAA, TAA, and DLAA often produce cleaner results.

docs.title: Can Miss Some Edges
docs.text: Since FXAA relies on contrast detection, some edges may remain jagged.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Method Quality Performance Blur FXAA Medium Excellent Medium MSAA High Medium Low TAA High Good Medium SSAA Very High Heavy None SMAA High Good Low

docs.title: When To Use FXAA
docs.text:
FXAA is a strong choice when:

  • You want maximum FPS
  • Your GPU is older or weaker
  • You play older games
  • You need lightweight anti-aliasing

docs.title: When To Avoid FXAA
docs.text:
You may prefer another method when:

  • You want maximum sharpness
  • You dislike blur
  • You have a strong GPU
  • Better AA options are available

docs.title: Common Games That Used FXAA
docs.text:
• Skyrim
  • Battlefield 3
  • Far Cry 3
  • Many Unreal Engine titles

docs.title: Final Summary
docs.text: FXAA is a fast and efficient anti-aliasing method that smooths jagged edges using image processing after rendering. It offers excellent performance with low GPU cost, but often introduces blur and lower image clarity compared to newer anti-aliasing technologies.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
There are a few words you should at least know the meaning of before you proceed to explore AA.

  • Deferred: Postponed to a later stage.
    • First pass — Draws all geometry and stores surface data (normals, albedo, depth) into the G-buffer.
    • Second pass — Runs lighting calculations on the G-buffer in screen space, after all geometry is done.
  • Types of AA: There are a few different types of AA and it is important to know the difference.
    • Spatial — Samples each pixel multiple times at different sub-pixel locations during rasterization. Produces high-quality results but increases memory and GPU cost (e.g. MSAA, SSAA).
    • Post-process — Applied as a screen-space image effect after the scene has been rendered. Fast and compatible with deferred pipelines, but can blur fine detail (e.g. FXAA, SMAA).
    • Temporal — Accumulates samples across multiple frames using motion vectors to reproject previous results. Industry standard for deferred pipelines; can cause ghosting on fast motion (e.g. TAA).
    • AI-based — Uses machine learning models to upscale or reconstruct a high-quality image from a lower-resolution input. Vendor-specific and typically the highest quality option (e.g. DLAA, DLSS, FSR).

docs.title: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA)
docs.text: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) is a hardware-accelerated technique used in real-time rendering to reduce the visual artifact known as aliasing — the "jagged edges" or "staircase" effect that appears on diagonal and curved geometry.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When a triangle is rasterized, the GPU must decide which pixels it covers. Without anti-aliasing, a pixel is either fully inside or fully outside the triangle — a binary decision that produces hard, jagged boundaries. MSAA solves this by sampling each pixel multiple times at sub-pixel locations and averaging the results to produce a smoother edge.

!!! info "Key Distinction" MSAA only runs the fragment shader once per pixel, but performs the depth and stencil test at every sub-sample. This makes it significantly cheaper than Super-Sample Anti-Aliasing (SSAA), which shades at every sample.

docs.title: 1. Sub-Sample Generation
docs.text:
For each pixel, the GPU generates N sample points arranged within the pixel's bounds (where N is the MSAA level, e.g. 2×, 4×, 8×). The exact positions follow a vendor-defined pattern designed to maximize coverage variety.

┌─────────────────┐
│  · ─ ─ ─ ─ · │   4× MSAA sample positions
│  │    ·        │   within a single pixel
│       │    ·  │
│  · ─ ─ ─ ─ · │
└─────────────────┘

docs.title: 2. Coverage and Depth Testing
docs.text: The GPU evaluates each sub-sample against the triangle's coverage and the depth buffer independently. A sub-sample is "covered" if it falls inside the triangle's projected area.

docs.title: 3. Fragment Shading
docs.text: The fragment shader runs once per pixel (not once per sample), using the centre of the pixel (or a centroid-interpolated position) to compute the colour output.

docs.title: 4. Resolve
docs.text: At the end of the frame, the multisample buffer is resolved: the N sample colours for each pixel are averaged into a single value, which is written to the final framebuffer.

docs.title: MSAA Levels
docs.text:
Level Samples per Pixel Performance Cost Edge Quality 2× 2 Low Moderate 4× 4 Medium Good 8× 8 High Very Good 16× 16 Very High Excellent

!!! tip 4× MSAA is the most common choice in games and real-time applications, balancing image quality with GPU memory and bandwidth cost.

docs.title: Memory and Bandwidth Impact
docs.text:
MSAA stores N depth, stencil, and colour samples per pixel in a multisample render target. This multiplies the render target's memory footprint by N:

  • A 1920×1080 RGBA8 framebuffer at 4× MSAA uses approximately 32 MB instead of 8 MB.
  • Bandwidth during the resolve pass increases proportionally.

!!! warning "Deferred Rendering Incompatibility" MSAA does not compose cleanly with deferred shading pipelines. The G-buffer stores per-pixel surface data, meaning MSAA sub-samples cannot be resolved before lighting is applied. Alternatives such as FXAA, TAA, or per-sample shading must be used instead.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
=== "OpenGL"

```c
// Request a multisample framebuffer from your windowing library (e.g. GLFW)
glfwWindowHint(GLFW_SAMPLES, 4);

// Enable multisampling
glEnable(GL_MULTISAMPLE);
```

=== "Vulkan"

```c
VkPipelineMultisampleStateCreateInfo multisampleState = {
    .sType                = VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_PIPELINE_MULTISAMPLE_STATE_CREATE_INFO,
    .rasterizationSamples = VK_SAMPLE_COUNT_4_BIT,
    .sampleShadingEnable  = VK_FALSE,
};
```

=== "Direct3D 11"

```cpp
DXGI_SWAP_CHAIN_DESC scDesc = {};
scDesc.SampleDesc.Count   = 4;   // 4× MSAA
scDesc.SampleDesc.Quality = 0;
```

=== "WebGPU"

```ts
const texture = device.createTexture({
  size: [canvas.width, canvas.height],
  sampleCount: 4,
  format: "bgra8unorm",
  usage: GPUTextureUsage.RENDER_ATTACHMENT,
});
```

docs.title: Per-Sample Shading
docs.text:
By default, the fragment shader runs once per pixel. You can opt into running it once per sample for higher quality, at a cost equal to SSAA:

=== "GLSL"

```glsl
// Force per-sample evaluation
in vec2 texCoord; // becomes per-sample when qualifier is used

layout(location = 0) out vec4 fragColor;

void main() {
    fragColor = texture(uTexture, texCoord);
}
```

=== "Vulkan"

```c
multisampleState.sampleShadingEnable  = VK_TRUE;
multisampleState.minSampleShading     = 1.0f; // shade at every sample
```

!!! note Per-sample shading is rarely needed in practice and defeats the primary performance advantage of MSAA.

docs.title: Centroid Interpolation
docs.text:
When a pixel is only partially covered by a triangle, interpolated varyings evaluated at the pixel centre may lie outside the triangle, producing artefacts. Centroid interpolation moves the evaluation point to the centroid of the covered samples, keeping it inside the triangle.

=== "GLSL"

```glsl
centroid in vec2 texCoord;
```

=== "HLSL"

```hlsl
centroid float2 texCoord : TEXCOORD0;
```

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Technique Type Works with Deferred? Notes SSAA Spatial Yes Highest quality, highest cost MSAA Spatial Poorly Best quality-to-cost for forward rendering FXAA Post-process Yes Fast, blurs fine detail SMAA Post-process Yes Better edge detection than FXAA TAA Temporal Yes Industry standard; requires motion vectors DLAA AI-based Yes High quality, vendor-specific

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• MSAA reduces geometric aliasing by testing coverage at multiple sub-pixel locations while keeping a single shading pass per pixel.
  • It is well-suited to forward rendering pipelines and natively supported by all major graphics APIs.
  • Choose your sample count based on your performance budget — 4× is the practical sweet spot for most applications.
  • For deferred pipelines or post-process stacks, consider TAA or SMAA instead.

docs.title: What is SSAA?
docs.text: Supersample Anti-Aliasing (SSAA), also known as Full-Scene Anti-Aliasing (FSAA), is a spatial anti-aliasing technique that renders the entire scene at a higher resolution than the display resolution, then downsamples (scales down) the result to fit the screen. This effectively increases the sampling rate per pixel, reducing aliasing artifacts. Instead of sampling once per pixel (point sampling), SSAA takes multiple samples within each pixel's area and averages them to produce the final pixel color.

docs.title: What is Aliasing?
docs.text: Aliasing occurs when a high-frequency signal is sampled at too low a frequency, causing different signals to become indistinguishable (aliases of each other).

docs.title: Visual Manifestations in Computer Graphics
docs.text:
• Jagged edges ("jaggies"): Staircase patterns on geometric edges
  • Moiré patterns: Interference patterns in fine textures
  • Temporal aliasing: Flickering and crawling artifacts in motion
  • Texture aliasing: Distortion in detailed textures at oblique angles

docs.title: The Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem
docs.text: To accurately reconstruct a signal, the sampling frequency must be at least twice the highest frequency component of the signal. In computer graphics, edges create infinite frequency signals, making perfect reconstruction theoretically impossible with finite sampling. This is where supersampling helps by increasing the effective sampling rate.

docs.title: Basic Process Flow
docs.text: The process follows three stages: Render at Higher Resolution → Downsample to Display Resolution → Display Final Image.

docs.title: Step 1: Upscaled Rendering
docs.text: The scene is rendered at a resolution higher than the display resolution by a factor (typically 2x, 4x, or 8x). For example, 4x SSAA on a 1920×1080 display renders at 3840×2160 (4 times the pixels), where each display pixel corresponds to a 2×2 grid of rendered samples.

docs.title: Step 2: Sample Pattern Configuration
docs.text:
Ordered Grid Sampling (OGSSAA) divides the display pixel area into a regular grid. For 4x SSAA this creates a 2x2 grid with four samples:

Rotated Grid Sampling (RGSSAA) places samples in a rotated diamond pattern which provides better edge anti-aliasing at specific angles, particularly near-horizontal and near-vertical edges.

Sparse Grid Sampling (SGSSAA) combines multiple sample patterns across adjacent pixels for more efficient coverage, sharing samples between neighboring pixels to reduce the total number of samples needed while maintaining quality.

docs.title: Step 3: Downsampling (Resolve)
docs.text: The high-resolution rendering is downsampled to the display resolution using a filter kernel. The Box Filter performs a simple average: final_color = (sample1 + sample2 + sample3 + sample4) / 4.0. The Gaussian Filter uses weighted averaging where center pixels receive more weight, producing smoother results. The Lanczos/Sinc Filter uses the sinc function sinc(x) = sin(πx) / (πx) for higher quality reconstruction that produces sharper results but may introduce slight ringing artifacts.

docs.title: TAA (Temporal Anti-Aliasing)
docs.text:
TAA is a modern anti-aliasing technique used in games to reduce jagged edges, shimmering, and flickering over time. Unlike FXAA or MSAA, TAA uses information from previous frames and combines it with the current frame to create a smoother and more stable image.

TAA is widely used in modern game engines because it improves motion stability and overall image quality.

docs.title: What Is Aliasing?
docs.text:
Aliasing happens when diagonal or curved edges appear jagged, or when small details flicker and shimmer during movement.

Common examples:

  • Stair-stepped edges
  • Fences shimmering in motion
  • Grass flickering
  • Thin lines crawling while moving camera

docs.title: Why TAA Was Created
docs.text:
Older methods solved only parts of aliasing:

  • MSAA helped polygon edges
  • FXAA was fast but blurry
  • Neither fully solved shimmering during motion

TAA was designed to provide:

  • Stable image during movement
  • Smooth edges
  • Reduced flicker
  • Better modern rendering support
  • Good balance of quality and performance

docs.title: How TAA Works
docs.text: TAA works across multiple frames instead of only one frame.

docs.title: Step 1: Slight Camera Jitter
docs.text:
Each frame is rendered with a tiny sub-pixel offset.

This gives different sample positions every frame.

Example:

Frame 1 sample position:

+

Frame 2 sample position:

  +

Frame 3 sample position:

 +

docs.title: Step 2: Save Previous Frame Data
docs.text: The engine stores image information from earlier frames.

docs.title: Step 3: Motion Vectors
docs.text:
The engine calculates where pixels moved between frames using motion vectors.

This helps align old frame data with the current frame.

docs.title: Step 4: Blend Frames Together
docs.text:
Current frame data is combined with previous frames.

This creates smoother edges and reduces flickering.

docs.title: Why It Is Called Temporal
docs.text:
The word temporal means related to time.

!!! info "Across Time" TAA improves image quality by using multiple frames over time instead of only the current frame.

docs.title: Performance Cost
docs.text:
TAA is usually efficient and popular in modern engines.

Typical impact:

  • Moderate GPU cost
  • Lower than SSAA
  • Often cheaper than high MSAA levels
  • Requires motion vector processing

docs.title: Excellent Motion Stability
docs.text: Reduces shimmering and crawling edges while moving.

docs.title: Smooth Edges
docs.text: Produces cleaner lines than many cheaper AA methods.

docs.title: Great For Modern Engines
docs.text: Works well with deferred rendering pipelines.

docs.title: Helps Thin Details
docs.text:
Improves:

  • Fences
  • Grass
  • Hair
  • Wires
  • Small geometry

docs.title: Blur / Softness
docs.text: TAA can make the image look softer.

docs.title: Ghosting
docs.text: Fast-moving objects may leave trails or smears.

docs.title: Input Clarity Loss
docs.text: Some players dislike reduced sharpness.

docs.title: Needs Good Implementation
docs.text: Poor TAA can look bad.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Method Quality Performance Blur Motion Stability FXAA Medium Excellent Medium Low MSAA High Medium None Medium TAA High Good Medium Excellent SSAA Very High Heavy None High SMAA High Good Low Medium

docs.title: When To Use TAA
docs.text:
TAA is a strong choice when:

  • You play modern AAA games
  • You want stable visuals while moving
  • You dislike shimmering
  • You use higher resolutions or detailed scenes

docs.title: When To Avoid TAA
docs.text:
You may prefer another method when:

  • You want maximum sharpness
  • You notice ghosting
  • You play competitive shooters
  • You dislike soft image quality

docs.title: Common Games That Use TAA
docs.text:
• Red Dead Redemption 2
  • Cyberpunk 2077
  • Elden Ring
  • Many Unreal Engine titles

docs.title: Final Summary
docs.text: TAA is a modern anti-aliasing method that combines current and previous frames to smooth edges and reduce flickering over time. It offers strong image stability and high quality, but can introduce blur and ghosting depending on implementation.

docs.title: Rasterization
docs.text: Rasterization is the foundation of real-time computer graphics. Unlike ray tracing, which simulates the physics of light, rasterization projects 3D geometry onto a 2D pixel grid. It is the primary technique used by GPUs for video games and interactive applications due to its high performance.

docs.title: The Geometry Stage
docs.text:
The process begins by transforming 3D vertex data through several coordinate spaces to determine where they sit on your screen.

  • Model → World Space: Positions objects within the global scene.
  • View Space: Reorients the world relative to the camera’s position.
  • Projection Space: Applies perspective, turning the 3D volume into a 2D coordinate system.

Vertex Shaders handle these transformations, allowing for effects like wind-blown grass or character skinning before the shape is "flattened."

docs.title: The Rasterization Step
docs.text:
Once the 2D coordinates of a triangle's vertices are determined, the hardware identifies which pixels fall within the triangle's boundaries.

  • Barycentric Interpolation: Used to smoothly blend data (like colors or textures) across the surface of the triangle between its three corners.
  • The Z-Buffer (Depth Testing): To solve the "visibility problem," the GPU stores the depth of every pixel. If a new triangle tries to draw over a pixel but is further away than what is already there, it is discarded.

!!! info "Performance Note" Rasterization's biggest strength is its "embarrassingly parallel" nature, allowing modern GPUs to process millions of triangles per second.

docs.title: The Fragment Shader
docs.text:
For every pixel identified during scan conversion, a Fragment Shader is executed to determine its final color.

  1. Texture Mapping: Sampling 2D images (diffuse, normal, and roughness maps) to add detail to geometry.
  2. Local Illumination: Using models like Blinn-Phong or PBR to calculate light interaction based on the surface normal.
  3. Alpha Blending: Handling transparency by mixing the fragment color with the existing background color.

docs.title: Global Effects (Approximations)
docs.text:
Because rasterizers process triangles in isolation, they cannot natively "see" other objects. To simulate complex light behavior, we use specialized buffers:

Technique Purpose How it works Shadow Mapping Shadows Renders the scene from the light's POV to see what is hidden. SSAO Ambient Occlusion Darkens cracks and corners based on the depth buffer. SSR Reflections Uses the pixels already on screen to "fake" reflections.

Weaknesses: Rasterization struggles with "off-screen" data. If a light source or reflecting object isn't currently visible to the camera, it usually disappears from the shadows or reflections.

docs.title: Ray Tracing
docs.text: Ray tracing is a rendering technique that simulates how light behaves in the real world by tracing the path of light rays as they interact with surfaces. Unlike rasterization which approximates lighting, ray tracing physically models reflection, refraction, shadows, and global illumination.

docs.title: Whitted Ray Tracing
docs.text:
Introduced by Turner Whitted in 1980 in his SIGGRAPH paper "An Improved Illumination Model for Shaded Display", this was the first recursive ray tracing algorithm and fundamentally changed how rendering was approached.

A primary ray is cast from the camera through each pixel into the scene. When it hits a surface, secondary rays are spawned recursively: - Shadow rays cast toward each light to check for occlusion - Reflection rays for mirror-like surfaces - Refraction rays for transparent surfaces using Snell's law and the surface's index of refraction

At diffuse surfaces, a standard illumination model like Phong is used. The algorithm recurses until it hits a diffuse surface or a maximum depth is reached.

Limitations: Whitted ray tracing only handles perfect specular reflection and refraction. It cannot simulate soft shadows, glossy reflections, depth of field, or motion blur since all rays travel in precise, single directions.

docs.title: Distributed Ray Tracing
docs.text:
Introduced by Robert Cook in 1984, distributed ray tracing extends Whitted by distributing ray directions stochastically according to the function they are sampling rather than firing a single precise ray.

By randomly distributing rays across: - Area lights → produces soft shadows with penumbras - Reflection lobes → produces glossy/blurry reflections - Camera aperture → produces depth of field - Time → produces motion blur - Lens → produces antialiasing naturally

This was a major step toward physically accurate rendering. Multiple rays are traced per pixel and averaged, so image quality increases with more samples at the cost of render time.

docs.title: Path Tracing
docs.text: Path tracing is an unbiased Monte Carlo rendering algorithm that solves the full rendering equation. Rather than recursively branching rays like Whitted, a single ray path is traced from the camera and bounced through the scene randomly according to the surface's BSDF until it either hits a light or is terminated by Russian Roulette. Many paths are traced per pixel and averaged to converge to a correct solution.

docs.title: Unidirectional Path Tracing
docs.text:
The standard form of path tracing. Paths are traced starting from the camera, bouncing off surfaces until they reach a light source. Simple to implement and works well in most scenes, but is inefficient in scenes with small or hard-to-reach light sources since most paths never find them.

Weaknesses: Caustics, interior scenes with small windows, and any lighting configuration where light paths are difficult to hit by chance from the camera.

docs.title: Bidirectional Path Tracing (BDPT)
docs.text:
Constructs two subpaths simultaneously — one from the camera and one from a light source — then attempts to connect them with a visibility ray in the middle. This dramatically improves efficiency in scenes where light is difficult to reach from the camera side alone.

BDPT is unbiased, meaning it converges to the mathematically correct solution with enough samples. It handles tricky lighting like interior scenes, indirect illumination, and caustics far more efficiently than unidirectional path tracing.

docs.title: Metropolis Light Transport (MLT)
docs.text:
MLT is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. Instead of sampling paths independently, it starts with a found light-carrying path and mutates it slightly to explore nearby paths. Paths that carry more light are sampled more frequently.

This makes MLT extremely efficient in difficult scenes with complex lighting — for example a scene lit only through a tiny crack, or a scene full of caustics where standard path tracing would rarely find any light-carrying paths at all.

Trade-off: MLT produces correlated noise rather than independent noise, which can look like splotchy artifacts. It is also harder to implement and parallelize than standard path tracing.

docs.title: Progressive Path Tracing
docs.text:
A refinement strategy rather than a distinct algorithm. The renderer continuously adds more samples per pixel, updating the image progressively in real time. Each new pass adds more information and the image visually converges from noisy to clean over time.

Used heavily in offline rendering applications like Blender's Cycles renderer, allowing artists to preview lighting interactively while the image refines in the background.

docs.title: Photon Mapping
docs.text:
A two-pass biased rendering algorithm introduced by Henrik Wann Jensen. In the first pass, photons are emitted from light sources and traced through the scene. When they hit diffuse surfaces their position, direction, and energy are stored in a spatial data structure called a photon map (typically a kd-tree).

In the second pass, rays are traced from the camera. At each surface intersection, nearby photons in the photon map are used to estimate the local irradiance via density estimation.

Photon mapping excels at caustics and scenes involving complex light transport that path tracing struggles with, such as light focusing through glass. It is a biased algorithm, meaning it does not converge to the exact correct solution, but it is consistent — accuracy increases with more photons.

Limitation: The entire photon map must be held in memory, placing a hard cap on quality.

docs.title: Progressive Photon Mapping (PPM)
docs.text:
Solves the memory limitation of standard photon mapping. PPM begins with a ray tracing pass from the camera, then iteratively shoots more and more photon passes, progressively refining the radiance estimate at each visible point.

Because the full photon map does not need to be stored — only statistics at hit points are accumulated — PPM can run with any desired accuracy using a fixed, limited amount of memory. It converges to the correct solution over time, making it practical for scenes with caustics and complex light transport where path tracing is inefficient.

docs.title: Volumetric Ray Tracing / Ray Marching
docs.text:
Used to render participating media — volumes where light scatters and absorbs as it travels through the medium, such as fog, smoke, clouds, fire, and subsurface skin.

A ray is marched in small steps through the volume. At each step the algorithm accounts for: - Absorption → light lost as it passes through the medium - Scattering → light deflected in a new direction - Emission → light emitted by the medium itself (fire, glowing gas)

Phase functions (such as Henyey-Greenstein) describe the angular distribution of scattered light. Volumetric ray tracing is computationally expensive and is typically combined with importance sampling and noise reduction techniques.

docs.title: Cone Tracing
docs.text:
Instead of an infinitely thin ray, a cone is traced through the scene. The cone expands as it travels, covering a larger area of the scene the farther it goes. This approximates anti-aliasing and filtering naturally since the cone footprint represents the solid angle being sampled.

Used in some global illumination approximations like voxel cone tracing (VXGI), where a voxelized representation of the scene is sampled with cones to estimate indirect lighting efficiently.

docs.title: Beam Tracing
docs.text:
A generalization of cone tracing that uses beams of arbitrary cross-sectional shape instead of cones. Beams can represent the exact projection of a pixel through the scene, accounting for all geometry they intersect rather than just the nearest hit.

Used in acoustic simulation and some specialized rendering contexts where full coverage of a beam's path matters.

docs.title: Irradiance Caching / Radiance Caching
docs.text:
A caching strategy to avoid recomputing expensive indirect lighting at every surface point. Irradiance is computed at a sparse set of points in the scene and interpolated for nearby points that have similar lighting conditions.

This provides a massive speedup for indirect diffuse lighting in offline rendering at the cost of some accuracy in areas with rapidly changing illumination. Radiance caching extends this idea to non-diffuse surfaces by caching directional radiance rather than just irradiance.

docs.title: Vertex Connection and Merging (VCM)
docs.text:
A unified algorithm that combines Bidirectional Path Tracing and Progressive Photon Mapping into a single framework using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). It automatically weights the contributions of both strategies to minimize noise.

VCM is particularly effective at specular-diffuse-specular (SDS) light paths — for example light reflecting off a mirror onto a diffuse floor and then into a glass object — which are difficult for either BDPT or photon mapping alone.

docs.title: Adjoint / Importance-Driven Path Tracing
docs.text:
Rather than tracing paths from the camera, adjoint methods trace paths from the light sources toward regions of importance (such as the camera or a specific region of interest). The adjoint of the rendering equation is solved instead of the forward equation.

This is mathematically equivalent to forward path tracing but can be more efficient in scenes where light transport from the source is more predictable than from the camera. Bidirectional methods combine both forward and adjoint tracing.

docs.title: Real-Time Ray Tracing (DXR / Vulkan RT)
docs.text:
Hardware-accelerated ray tracing introduced with NVIDIA's Turing architecture (RTX 20 series) in 2018. Exposed through Microsoft's DirectX Raytracing (DXR) API and Vulkan's VK_KHR_ray_tracing extension.

Dedicated hardware units called RT Cores handle bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) traversal and ray-triangle intersection tests, offloading this from shader cores. This makes selective ray tracing feasible in real-time at interactive framerates.

In games, full path tracing is still too expensive so ray tracing is typically used selectively for specific effects: - Ray-traced shadows - Ray-traced reflections - Ray-traced ambient occlusion - Ray-traced global illumination

These are blended with rasterized geometry to produce a hybrid result. Denoising (using AI denoisers like NVIDIA DLSS or dedicated NRD denoisers) is essential since only a very small number of rays per pixel can be traced in real time.

docs.title: Game Engines and Their Ray Tracing Types
Godot (4.x)
docs.text: Godot does not have built-in hardware ray tracing support. Its rendering is based on rasterization with screen-space techniques for reflections and ambient occlusion. External ray tracing solutions or custom render plugins could theoretically be integrated but there is no official ray tracing pipeline in Godot as of version 4.x.

docs.title: Unity
docs.text: Unity's ray tracing is exclusive to the High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP). It requires a DXR-capable GPU (NVIDIA RTX or AMD RDNA2+) and DirectX 12.

docs.title: Ray-Traced Ambient Occlusion (RTAO)
docs.text: Replaces screen-space AO with physically accurate ambient occlusion computed by tracing rays into the hemisphere above each surface point. Produces correct occlusion in corners, crevices, and around objects without the screen-space artifacts of SSAO.

docs.title: Ray-Traced Reflections (RTR)
docs.text: Replaces screen-space reflections (SSR) with ray-traced reflections that correctly reflect geometry off-screen, at grazing angles, and behind the camera. Supports roughness for glossy reflections.

docs.title: Ray-Traced Global Illumination (RTGI)
docs.text: Computes indirect diffuse lighting by tracing rays into the scene from each surface and gathering incoming light. Produces accurate color bleeding and bounce lighting that baked lightmaps or probes cannot match for dynamic scenes.

docs.title: Ray-Traced Shadows
docs.text: Traces shadow rays toward area lights to produce physically correct soft shadows with accurate penumbras based on light size and distance. Replaces shadow maps which cannot represent soft shadows accurately.

docs.title: Path Tracer
docs.text: A full offline-quality path tracer available in HDRP for producing ground-truth reference images. Not intended for real-time gameplay but used for cinematic renders, look development, and reference comparisons.

docs.title: Lumen (UE5's Default GI System)
docs.text:
Lumen is UE5's fully dynamic global illumination and reflections system. It operates using a hybrid approach — screen traces for nearby geometry and hardware ray tracing or signed distance field (SDF) traces for distant geometry, all feeding into a surface cache that stores and reuses lighting data.

Lumen provides real-time indirect lighting, color bleeding, and reflections that update dynamically as lights and geometry change, without baking. It scales from software-only mode (no RT hardware required) to full hardware ray tracing mode for higher quality.

docs.title: Legacy / Explicit Hardware Ray Tracing Effects (UE4 / UE5)
docs.text:
Available since UE4.22, these are direct per-effect hardware ray tracing features that can be enabled individually in the post process volume: - Ray-Traced Shadows - Ray-Traced Reflections - Ray-Traced Ambient Occlusion - Ray-Traced Translucency - Ray-Traced Global Illumination (RTGI, largely superseded by Lumen in UE5)

These give artists explicit control over which effects use ray tracing, useful when Lumen's automatic approach does not fit the project's needs.

docs.title: Path Tracer
docs.text: UE5 includes a full hardware path tracer for offline-quality rendering, used for cinematic shots, archviz, and reference rendering. It uses progressive accumulation and converges to a physically correct solution over many frames. In UE5.4+ it supports Nanite geometry for film-quality geometric detail.

docs.title: NVIDIA RTX Branch (NvRTX)
docs.text:
NvRTX is a custom fork of Unreal Engine maintained by NVIDIA on GitHub, containing the latest experimental and production ray tracing technologies ahead of their inclusion in the main UE branch. It is fully compatible with the corresponding UE version.

Key technologies included in NvRTX:

  • RTXGI (RTX Global Illumination) — Computes infinite multi-bounce indirect lighting and soft shadow occlusion dynamically without bake times or light leaks. Available in NvRTX 4.27 and 5.0.
  • RTXDI (RTX Direct Illumination) — Allows an unlimited number of dynamic shadow-casting lights in a scene at fixed GPU cost using reservoir-based importance sampling (ReSTIR).
  • DLSS (Deep Learning Super Sampling) — AI-based upscaling that renders at a lower resolution and uses a neural network to reconstruct a higher resolution image, recovering much of the performance cost of ray tracing.
  • NRD (NVIDIA Real-Time Denoisers) — A denoising library specifically designed for real-time ray traced outputs, reducing the noise from low sample counts to a clean image.
  • RTX Mega Geometry — Introduced in NvRTX 5.6, this allows real-time path tracing of Nanite-level geometry by clustering millions of triangles into reusable structures, reducing CPU overhead and VRAM usage in heavy ray traced scenes.
  • Enhanced Ray Traced Translucency — Improved handling of transparent and translucent surfaces under ray tracing, addressing limitations in standard UE translucency rendering.

NvRTX can increase hardware ray traced and path traced operations by up to 40% compared to the standard UE branch on compatible NVIDIA hardware.
